issues.title: Single underscore include guard used
issues.description: The rule requires header files to use include guards with double underscores at the start (e.g., __FILENAME_H), but the code uses a single underscore prefix instead (_REDIS_H)
issues.rule_name: Header Files Must Use Double-Underscore Include Guards

issues.title: Unsigned integer wraparound in AOF corruption size check
issues.description: The size comparison casts both operands to size_t (unsigned), which causes undefined behavior when valid_up_to exceeds sb.st_size. In this edge case, the subtraction sb.st_size - valid_up_to produces a negative value that wraps around to a very large unsigned integer, always exceeding aof_load_broken_max_size. This prevents automatic recovery even when the corruption is actually small, causing the server to fail to start when it should recover successfully.

issues.title: Incorrect early exit prevents loading incremental AOF after successful base recovery
issues.description: The error handling condition incorrectly treats AOF_BROKEN_RECOVERED as a failure state, causing the function to exit immediately after successfully recovering a corrupted base AOF file. When a base AOF is the last file and gets successfully recovered (ret == AOF_BROKEN_RECOVERED), the server should continue to load any incremental AOF files. However, this bug causes an early exit to cleanup, preventing incremental files from being loaded and potentially losing data. The correct behavior is to only exit on AOF_OPEN_ERR or AOF_FAILED, not on successful recovery.

pr.title: Code Review Bench PR #14058 - Add auto-repair options for broken AOF tail on startup

structured_output.summary:
This PR adds two opt-in startup options, `aof-load-broken` (default `no`) and `aof-load-broken-max-size` (default 4096 bytes). When the AOF loader hits a format error ("Bad file format"), and the bytes from the last good command to EOF are under the threshold, it truncates the file at the last valid offset and continues loading. It reuses the existing `AOF_TRUNCATED` plumbing: a new `AOF_BROKEN_RECOVERED` return code, the same last-file-only rule, and the same `valid_up_to` bookkeeping that `aof-load-truncated` already uses. Config wiring, `redis.conf` docs, and integration tests are included.

The feature is reasonable in intent and the opt-in default is the right call. However, I found a data-loss bug in the truncation logic. `valid_up_to` is never set after the RDB preamble is loaded, so when no AOF command has parsed yet it stays at 0. The format-error path then calls `truncate(path, 0)` on the whole file, which deletes the preamble. Separately, truncation happens inside `loadSingleAppendOnlyFile` before the caller decides that a non-last file is a fatal error, so a corrupted middle file is destroyed on disk even though the server refuses to start. The tests also have gaps: `wait_for_log_messages` matches on any single pattern, and one test deletes the manifest along with the incr files.
structured_output.verdictRationale: The truncate-to-zero path can silently delete an entire small RDB-preamble base AOF on startup. That is a data-loss bug in an opt-in feature, so it has to be fixed before merge. The non-last-file truncation and the test gaps should also be addressed. The core approach and the config/docs are sound.

architecture.overview:
Today, AOF loading lives in `src/aof.c`. `loadDataFromDisk()` in `server.c` calls `loadAppendOnlyFiles()`, which walks the manifest's base file and then its incr files. Each file is replayed by `loadSingleAppendOnlyFile()`, which tracks `valid_up_to`, the byte offset of the last fully applied command. Two error labels exist. `uxeof` handles a short read and, when `aof-load-truncated` is on, truncates at `valid_up_to` and returns `AOF_TRUNCATED`. `fmterr` handles a malformed line and always fails. The caller accepts a truncated file only if it is the last file in the manifest.

This PR adds a parallel path for `fmterr`. When `aof-load-broken` is on and `sb.st_size - valid_up_to` is below `aof-load-broken-max-size`, the loader truncates at `valid_up_to` and returns the new `AOF_BROKEN_RECOVERED` code. It also widens `valid_up_to` tracking to cover the new option, and makes the caller treat the new code the same as `AOF_TRUNCATED`. The config options are registered in `config.c` and the two `server` fields are declared in `server.h`.
steps: Start at `loadDataFromDisk()` in `src/server.c`. It calls `loadAppendOnlyFiles()` and exits only on `AOF_FAILED` or `AOF_OPEN_ERR`.

In `loadAppendOnlyFiles()` (`src/aof.c`), the base file is loaded first, then each incr file. The new `AOF_BROKEN_RECOVERED` code is accepted only when the file is the last one. Otherwise it is converted to `AOF_FAILED`.

In `loadSingleAppendOnlyFile()`, `valid_up_to` is updated after each successfully applied command when either truncation option is on. The RDB-preamble branch does not update it, which matters for the finding below.

The new logic lives in the `fmterr:` block. It truncates the file to `valid_up_to` and jumps to `loaded_ok` if the tail is small enough. The truncation happens before the caller's last-file check, which is the ordering problem described in the findings.
Config and docs: the options are registered in `src/config.c`, declared in `src/server.h`, documented in `redis.conf`, and exercised by new cases in `tests/integration/aof.tcl`.

findings.title: RDB-preamble base can be truncated to zero bytes, deleting the whole base
findings.fixPrompt: In `src/aof.c` `loadSingleAppendOnlyFile()`, the RDB-preamble branch (around line 1550) never sets `valid_up_to`, so it stays 0. The new `fmterr:` recovery (lines ~1725-1728) then truncates the whole file to 0 bytes when the file is under `aof-load-broken-max-size`. Fix both: set `valid_up_to = ftello(fp)` after `rdbLoadRio` succeeds, and make the `fmterr` recovery refuse to truncate when there is no valid command boundary past the preamble (for example, only recover when `valid_up_to` is at least the preamble end, or fail with the original "Bad file format" message). Match the existing `valid_up_to == -1` guard style. Add an integration test where the base is an RDB preamble followed by a garbage tail under the threshold, and assert the preamble data survives.

findings.title: Corrupted non-last AOF is truncated on disk before the server refuses to start
findings.fixPrompt: In `src/aof.c`, the `fmterr:` recovery in `loadSingleAppendOnlyFile()` (lines ~1725-1728) truncates the AOF before the caller's last-file check in `loadAppendOnlyFiles()` (lines ~1836-1842 and ~1870-1874). When a non-last file is corrupt, the file is mutated on disk and the server then refuses to start. Move the truncation so it only runs when the file is the last one: either pass a `last_file` flag into `loadSingleAppendOnlyFile()`, or return `AOF_BROKEN_RECOVERED` without truncating and perform the truncate in `loadAppendOnlyFiles()` after the last-file check. Keep the existing `aof-load-truncated` behavior unchanged, or apply the same fix there and call it out. Update the integration test that swaps mid and last files so it also checks that the mid file content is unchanged after the failed start.

findings.title: stopLoading() reports failure for a successful broken-tail recovery
findings.fixPrompt: In `src/aof.c` `loadAppendOnlyFiles()`, the cleanup label (around line 1894) calls `stopLoading(ret == AOF_OK || ret == AOF_TRUNCATED)`. Add `ret == AOF_BROKEN_RECOVERED` to that condition so a successful broken-tail recovery is reported as a successful load to modules, matching how `AOF_TRUNCATED` is handled.

findings.title: Log-message wait helper passes if any one expected message appears
findings.fixPrompt: In `tests/integration/aof.tcl`, the new `aof-load-broken` tests use `wait_for_log_messages` with multiple patterns (around lines 714-720 and 817-823). That helper returns on any single match, so the tests do not check all expected messages. Split these into separate `wait_for_log_messages` calls, one per expected message, or assert each. In the "Intermediate AOF is broken" test, also assert that the mid AOF file was truncated to the valid prefix (its size or content) after the failed start, so the test actually exercises the recovery and the truncation side effect. Likewise, the "Corrupted last AOF file: should still start and recover" test (around lines 833-838) should assert that the recovery log line is present, not just that `fo` equals "mid".

findings.title: Test cleanup glob also deletes the AOF manifest
findings.body:
At line 724, `exec rm -f $aof_dirpath/appendonly.aof.*` is meant to remove the incr files. The glob also matches `appendonly.aof.manifest`, which is `$aof_manifest_file` at line 9. No manifest is recreated before `start_server_aof` runs on the next line, so the "Corrupted base AOF (last file): should recover" test depends on how the server rebuilds state without a manifest. The test may pass for reasons unrelated to the change.

::code{file="tests/integration/aof.tcl" lines="722-727"}
findings.fixPrompt: In `tests/integration/aof.tcl` at the `exec rm -f $aof_dirpath/appendonly.aof.*` line (~724), the glob also removes `appendonly.aof.manifest`. Remove only the incr files explicitly, for example by deleting `$aof_file` and any other incr files by name, or rewrite the manifest so it lists only the base file (using `create_aof_manifest`, as done later in the file). Then check that the "param should be 'ok'" assertion is exercising the base-file recovery path and not a missing-manifest startup.

findings.title: Unrelated include-guard rename in server.h
findings.body:
The PR renames `__REDIS_H` to `_REDIS_H` in `src/server.h`. That has nothing to do with AOF recovery. Identifiers beginning with a double underscore are reserved, so the rename may be a legitimate cleanup, but it does not belong in this change. It expands the review surface and makes history harder to read.

::diff{file="src/server.h" lines="15-16"}
findings.fixPrompt: In `src/server.h`, revert the include-guard rename from `_REDIS_H` back to `__REDIS_H`. Keep this PR limited to the AOF recovery changes. If the guard rename is wanted, submit it as a separate PR.

findings.title: Recovery treats any mid-file format error as a tail, dropping valid commands
findings.body:
The option is named and documented as recovering a corrupted tail. The code does not check whether the bad bytes are at the end of the file. The check is only that `sb.st_size - valid_up_to` is under the threshold. If a bad line sits in the middle of the file and is followed by a few KB of valid commands, all of those commands are silently dropped and the log says "AOF loaded anyway". The `redis.conf` text does say it handles format errors in the middle, but the option name and the power-loss rationale both point at tails.

This is a behavior trade-off rather than a defect. It is worth stating explicitly in the log line, and possibly in the docs, that trailing valid commands past the bad line are discarded.
findings.fixPrompt: In `src/aof.c` `fmterr:` (lines ~1725-1737), the broken-tail recovery truncates at `valid_up_to` even when valid commands follow the bad line. Decide whether this is acceptable. If it is, make the recovery log say how many bytes were discarded and that they may contain valid commands. If it is not, detect whether the bad bytes extend to EOF (for example, by checking that no later `*` line parses) before truncating. Update the `redis.conf` comment to match the chosen behavior.

findings.title: Recovery is opt-in with a conservative default
findings.body: `aof-load-broken` defaults to `no` in both `redis.conf` and `src/config.c`. The threshold defaults to 4 KB and is in bytes, so the feature stays off unless the operator enables it. The `redis.conf` block explains the data-loss trade-off clearly, and the `aof-load-broken-max-size` setting gives a bound on how much can be dropped.

findings.title: Reuses the existing AOF_TRUNCATED machinery
findings.body: The new code path reuses `valid_up_to`, the last-file rule, and the `loaded_ok` label. It does not introduce a new loader or a second truncation mechanism. The change is small and easy to read next to `uxeof`. The remaining problems are about ordering and the preamble edge case, not about structure.
